decisions.title: Idle Polling Is the Autonomy Entry Point
decisions.description: During idle cycles, a worker checks inboxes, task boards, and pending requests to discover whether something can be claimed. This polling is the fundamental mechanism of autonomy: without a new user input, the agent still finds work to do. The polling interval balances responsiveness against resource usage.
decisions.alternatives: Event-driven notification (push-based) is more responsive but adds subscription complexity. Having the lead explicitly assign all work eliminates autonomy entirely. Polling is the simplest mechanism that enables self-directed work.

decisions.title: Claim Rules Must Stay Explicit and Bounded
decisions.description: The system defines clear rules for what a worker may claim: only tasks matching its role, only unclaimed tasks, and only one task at a time. Collision avoidance uses atomic file-based claims (write claim file, verify exclusive ownership). Back-off rules prevent a worker from hammering the board when nothing is available.
decisions.alternatives: Allowing unrestricted claims leads to collisions and duplicate work. Using a central dispatcher eliminates autonomy. A distributed lock system adds infrastructure complexity.

decisions.title: Resume Depends on Visible State, Not Hidden Context
decisions.description: A worker does not continue from nowhere. It resumes from task state, protocol state, mailbox contents, and its own role state. All of this is persisted to disk, so the worker can recover its context even after a crash or context compression. This is why earlier chapters invested in durable records: autonomy depends on them.
decisions.alternatives: Resuming from compressed summaries is unreliable because summaries may have lost critical state. Keeping all state in memory prevents recovery after crashes. Visible, persistent state files are the foundation for safe self-resume.
